claims.claim: Mazin Saleem notes that Le Guin repeatedly uses the modal 'may' when the book describes a Kesh custom.
claims.quote: Again and again, Le Guin used the word

claims.claim: Saleem quotes a Kesh description of a ritual song whose permitted repetitions are given as an open list ending in the option of not at all.
claims.source: Mazin Saleem quoting Always Coming Home, Strange Horizons, 2018
claims.quote: it may be sung four times, or five times, or nine times

claims.claim: Saleem reports that the book's own note offers two competing readings of a disputed Kesh text rather than a verdict.
claims.source: Mazin Saleem quoting Always Coming Home, Strange Horizons, 2018
claims.quote: a vengeful biography pretending to be autobiography

claims.claim: Saleem describes a gloss attached to a Kesh story as spoken by a commentator on that story in the present tense.
claims.quote: writes a commentator on the story

claims.claim: Saleem gives the length of Always Coming Home as 525 pages and lists field notes first among its contents.
claims.quote: At 525 pages, including field notes, stories, maps, charts

claims.claim: Garlick and King describe the Back of the Book as encyclopaedia-like appendices holding the novel's practical information.
claims.source: Ben Garlick and Liesl King, cultural geographies, 2022
claims.quote: appendices referred to as ‘The Back of the Book’

claims.claim: Garlick and King characterise Pandora as an implicit translator or reporter rather than a character with a stake in the events.
claims.source: Ben Garlick and Liesl King, cultural geographies, 2022

claims.claim: A Kesh social fact is stated in Always Coming Home as a rule of the language's grammar.
claims.source: Le Guin, Always Coming Home, quoted in Garlick and King, cultural geographies, 2022
claims.quote: Kesh grammar makes no provision for a relation of ownership

claims.claim: Kesh social disapproval is reported in Always Coming Home as an agentless past passive listing three disapproved things.
claims.source: Le Guin, Always Coming Home, quoted in Garlick and King, cultural geographies, 2022
claims.quote: a competitive attitude were all socially disapproved

claims.claim: Garlick and King report the Kesh life expectancy from the novel as a range of thirty to forty years.
claims.source: Ben Garlick and Liesl King, cultural geographies, 2022

claims.claim: Danny Yee describes the Back of the Book as presenting the Kesh in a more traditional ethnographic form than the rest of the volume.
claims.source: Danny Yee, review of Always Coming Home, 1995
claims.quote: contains additional information about the Kesh in more traditional ethnographic form

claims.claim: The Ekumen field notes in The Left Hand of Darkness state a biological rule in the present tense with a generic plural subject.
claims.source: Le Guin, The Left Hand of Darkness ch. 7, quoted in Nick Hubble's BSFA Review notice
claims.quote: Normal individuals have no predisposition to either sexual role in kemmer

claims.claim: The same field notes mark the limit of the observer's own experience in a first-person parenthesis.
claims.source: Le Guin, The Left Hand of Darkness ch. 7, quoted in Nick Hubble's BSFA Review notice
claims.quote: I haven’t seen this done in rural Karhide

claims.claim: The field notes cite a second named observer inside a parenthesis before qualifying his report.
claims.source: Le Guin, The Left Hand of Darkness ch. 7, quoted in Nick Hubble's BSFA Review notice
claims.quote: Otie Nim wrote that in the Orgoreyn region the use

claims.claim: The field notes close the ambisexuality section with a twelve-word sentence built entirely of common kinship nouns.
claims.source: Le Guin, The Left Hand of Darkness ch. 7, quoted in Nick Hubble's BSFA Review notice
claims.quote: the mother of several children may be the father of several more
